title: Simple Machines
description: Simple machines and mechanisms from wheels and ramps to robots: pushes and pulls, wheels, ramps, levers, pulleys, the six simple machines, gears, mechanical advantage and work, compound machines, engines and efficiency, and robotics, control systems and automation.

lessons.title: Why Wheels Roll
objectives: Find wheels on everyday things
Explain that wheels make moving things easier
explanation: A wheel is round, so it can roll smoothly. Rolling is much easier than sliding or dragging.
Wheels are on cars, bicycles, trains, prams, shopping trolleys, office chairs and suitcases. They help us move heavy things with less effort.
The wheel is one of the oldest and most important inventions — people have used wheels for more than 5,000 years!

vocabulary.meaning: to move by turning over and over
to pull something along the ground

examples: A suitcase with wheels is easier to pull.
A toy car rolling across the floor.

lessons.title: Up the Ramp
objectives: Explain how a ramp helps move things up
Compare steep and gentle ramps
explanation: A ramp is a sloping surface that joins a low place to a high place. It is easier to push a heavy thing up a ramp than to lift it straight up.
A gentle (less steep) ramp is easier to push up but longer. A steep ramp is shorter but harder.
Ramps help people using wheelchairs and prams get into buildings. Things also roll down ramps faster when they are steeper.

vocabulary.meaning: a sloping surface between low and high places

examples: A wheelchair ramp at a hospital.

story.text: Ivaan made two ramps with books and boards: one steep, one gentle. He let two toy cars go at the same time. Zoom! The car on the steep ramp shot off first. "Steep is fast going down," he said. Then he tried pushing a block up each ramp. "But gentle is easier going up!"

lessons.title: Lift With a Lever
objectives: Name the load, effort and fulcrum on a lever
Show that moving the fulcrum changes how easy lifting is
explanation: A lever is a stiff bar that turns on a point called the fulcrum. The thing you lift is the load; the push you give is the effort.
A seesaw is a lever! If a heavier person sits closer to the middle, a lighter person can balance them by sitting further away.
Putting the fulcrum close to the load makes it easier to lift. Levers around us include spoons used to open tin lids, bottle openers and scissors.

vocabulary.meaning: a stiff bar that turns on a point

examples: A seesaw in the park.
A spoon prising open a tin lid.

story.text: Papa sat on one end of the seesaw. Ivaan sat on the other end — and nothing happened! Papa was too heavy. Then Papa slid closer to the middle. Ivaan went down and Papa went up! "Moving closer to the fulcrum made me lighter on the lever," Papa explained. Ivaan felt as strong as a giant.

lessons.title: Pulling Down to Lift Up
objectives: Explain how a single pulley changes the direction of a pull
Describe where pulleys are used
explanation: A pulley is a wheel with a groove that holds a rope. When you pull down on one end of the rope, the load on the other end goes up!
A single fixed pulley changes the direction of the pull — pulling down is easier than lifting up because you can use your body weight.
Using several pulleys together (a block and tackle) reduces the effort needed. Pulleys are used in wells, flagpoles, cranes and lifts.

vocabulary.meaning: a wheel with a grooved rim for a rope

examples: Drawing water from a village well.
Raising the flag on Independence Day.

lessons.title: The Six Simple Machines
objectives: Name and describe the six simple machines
Identify simple machines in everyday tools
explanation: There are six classical simple machines: the lever, the wheel and axle, the pulley, the inclined plane (ramp), the wedge and the screw.

A wedge is two inclined planes back to back — like an axe or knife — that splits things apart. A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder; turning it moves it in or lifts things, like a jar lid or a bolt.

A wheel and axle is a big wheel fixed to a smaller rod (axle) — turning the big wheel turns the axle with more force, as in a door knob or a steering wheel. Simple machines make work easier by changing the size or direction of a force.

vocabulary.meaning: two inclined planes that split things
an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder
a rod that a wheel turns on

examples: An axe as a wedge.
A door knob as a wheel and axle.

"Six out of six!" she shouted, out of breath.

lessons.title: Teeth That Turn
objectives: Explain how meshed gears turn in opposite directions
Describe how gear size changes speed
explanation: A gear is a wheel with teeth. When two gears mesh (their teeth fit together), turning one turns the other — in the opposite direction.
If a big gear turns a small gear, the small gear spins faster. If a small gear turns a big gear, the big gear turns more slowly but with more force.
Gears are in bicycles (using a chain), clocks, washing machines and cars. On a bicycle, a low gear makes pedalling uphill easier.
examples: Bicycle gears for going uphill.
Tiny gears inside a wind-up clock.

story.title: The Bicycle Hill
story.text: Kiko pedalled hard up the hill, puffing. His cousin called, "Change to a lower gear!" Kiko clicked the lever, and suddenly pedalling was much easier — though his legs went round faster and the bike moved slower. "Gears trade speed for force," his cousin said. Kiko reached the top grinning.

lessons.title: No Free Lunch
objectives: Calculate work and mechanical advantage
Classify levers into three classes
explanation: In science, work is done when a force moves something: work = force × distance, measured in joules. Simple machines don't reduce the work needed — they trade force for distance. A ramp needs less force but a longer distance.

Mechanical advantage (MA) = load ÷ effort. If you lift a 600 N load with 200 N of effort, MA = 3. For an ideal lever, MA also equals effort arm ÷ load arm. Archimedes said, "Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth."

Levers come in three classes: first class (fulcrum in the middle — seesaw), second class (load in the middle — wheelbarrow), third class (effort in the middle — tweezers, your forearm). Third-class levers have MA less than 1 but increase speed and range of motion.

vocabulary.meaning: the unit of work and energy

examples: A wheelbarrow (second-class lever).
Your forearm lifting a cup (third-class lever).

story.title: Archimedes and the Ship
story.text: An ancient story tells that Archimedes of Syracuse used a system of levers and pulleys to drag a fully loaded ship onto shore single-handed, astonishing King Hiero. Whether or not it happened exactly so, the principle was real: with enough mechanical advantage, a small force can move a huge load.

lessons.title: Machines Inside Machines
objectives: Identify simple machines within compound machines
Design a chain-reaction machine
explanation: A compound machine combines two or more simple machines. Scissors are two levers with wedge blades. A bicycle uses wheels and axles, levers (brakes, pedals), gears and screws.
Cranes combine pulleys, levers and winches. An excavator uses hydraulic systems with levers to dig.

Rube Goldberg machines, named after an American cartoonist, are deliberately complicated chain-reaction machines that perform a simple task in many steps — great for learning how energy passes from one part to the next.

vocabulary.meaning: a machine made of two or more simple machines
a series of events each causing the next

examples: Scissors: levers plus wedges.

lessons.title: No Machine Is Perfect
objectives: Describe energy transfers and losses in machines
Calculate efficiency as a percentage
explanation: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred — the law of conservation of energy. In machines, some energy is always transferred to less useful forms, mostly heat from friction, and sound.
Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input × 100%. If a motor uses 500 J and does 400 J of useful work, it is 80% efficient. No real machine is 100% efficient.

Engineers increase efficiency by reducing friction (lubricants, ball bearings, streamlining). A typical petrol car engine converts only around 20–35% of fuel energy into motion, while electric motors are often over 85% efficient.

vocabulary.meaning: useful output divided by total input
energy is not created or destroyed

examples: Oiling a squeaky bicycle chain.
Ball bearings in a skateboard wheel.

story.title: The Squeaky Wheel
story.text: Kiko's bicycle squeaked and felt hard to pedal. His uncle dripped oil onto the chain and wheel bearings. Suddenly the bike glided silently. "The squeak was energy escaping as sound and heat," his uncle said. "Now more of your effort goes into moving forward."

lessons.title: How Engines Work
objectives: Explain how steam, combustion and electric engines produce motion
Evaluate the environmental impact of engines
explanation: A steam engine burns fuel to boil water; the expanding steam pushes a piston. James Watt's improvements in the 1760s–1780s, including a separate condenser, made steam engines far more efficient, powering the Industrial Revolution. India's first passenger train ran from Bori Bunder to Thane in 1853.

An internal combustion engine burns fuel inside cylinders. In a four-stroke engine: intake (fuel and air enter), compression, power (a spark ignites the mixture, pushing the piston) and exhaust. The pistons turn a crankshaft.

Electric motors use magnetism: a current in a coil within a magnetic field creates a turning force. Electric vehicles produce no exhaust at the tailpipe, but their overall impact depends on how the electricity is generated.

vocabulary.meaning: a part that moves up and down in a cylinder
a shaft turning up-and-down motion into rotation

examples: A steam locomotive on a heritage railway.

lessons.title: Sense, Think, Act
objectives: Describe the sense-think-act cycle of a robot
Explain open-loop and closed-loop control
explanation: A robot senses its environment with sensors (light, distance, touch, cameras), processes information with a controller (a computer) and acts with actuators (motors, servos, grippers).

An open-loop system acts without checking results — a simple toaster timer. A closed-loop (feedback) system measures its output and adjusts — a thermostat turns heating on and off to keep a set temperature. Cruise control and self-balancing robots use feedback.

A common controller is PID (proportional-integral-derivative), which adjusts based on the current error, past errors and how fast the error is changing. Robots are used in factories, surgery, warehouses and space — ISRO's Pragyan rover explored the Moon in 2023.
examples: A line-following robot using light sensors.
A thermostat as a feedback system.

story.title: The Robot That Kept Falling
story.text: Meera's two-wheeled robot kept toppling over. She added a gyroscope sensor and wrote feedback code: if tilting forward, drive forward slightly; if tilting back, reverse. It wobbled wildly at first. She tuned the numbers in her controller patiently. Finally, it balanced — rocking gently like a person standing on a bus.

lessons.title: Machines, Jobs and the Future
objectives: Trace the history of industrial automation
Evaluate automation's effects on work and society
explanation: The First Industrial Revolution (late 1700s) mechanised production with water and steam. The Second (late 1800s) brought electricity and assembly lines — Henry Ford's moving assembly line (1913) cut car assembly time dramatically. Later waves added computers and, now, AI and connected systems.

Automation increases productivity and can remove dangerous, dull or dirty tasks. But it can also displace workers. In the early 1800s, Luddites in England smashed textile machinery that threatened their livelihoods. Economists debate whether new technologies create more jobs than they destroy and who benefits.

Responses include education and retraining, social safety nets, and designing technology to support workers. Safety standards govern how robots work alongside humans (collaborative robots, or "cobots").

vocabulary.meaning: using machines to do tasks without human effort
a 19th-century worker who opposed textile machines
a robot designed to work alongside people

examples: Car factories with robotic welding arms.
Cobots helping workers lift heavy parts.

story.title: The Handloom and the Power Loom
story.text: In 19th-century India, cheap machine-made cloth from British mills flooded markets, and many handloom weavers lost their livelihoods. Later, Gandhi's khadi movement promoted hand-spinning partly in response. The story shows that automation's effects depend on who controls the machines and who shares the gains.
